16:103.ar: وَلَقَدۡ نَعۡلَمُ أَنَّهُمۡ يَقُولُونَ إِنَّمَا يُعَلِّمُهُۥ بَشَرࣱۗ لِّسَانُ ٱلَّذِي يُلۡحِدُونَ إِلَيۡهِ أَعۡجَمِيࣱّ وَهَٰذَا لِسَانٌ عَرَبِيࣱّ مُّبِينٌ
16:103.en: And We know well that they say: Only a man teacheth him. The speech of him at whom they falsely hint is outlandish, and this is clear Arabic speech

25:5.ar: وَقَالُوٓاْ أَسَٰطِيرُ ٱلۡأَوَّلِينَ ٱكۡتَتَبَهَا فَهِيَ تُمۡلَىٰ عَلَيۡهِ بُكۡرَةࣰ وَأَصِيلࣰ ا
25:5.en: And they say: Fables of the men of old which he hath had written down so that they are dictated to him morn and evening

111:1.en: The power of Abu Lahab will perish, and he will perish

111:2.ar: مَآ أَغۡنَىٰ عَنۡهُ مَالُهُۥ وَمَا كَسَبَ
111:2.en: His wealth and gains will not exempt him

111:3.en: He will be plunged in flaming Fire

111:5.en: Will have upon her neck a halter of palm-fibre

8:44.ar: وَإِذۡ يُرِيكُمُوهُمۡ إِذِ ٱلۡتَقَيۡتُمۡ فِيٓ أَعۡيُنِكُمۡ قَلِيلࣰ ا وَيُقَلِّلُكُمۡ فِيٓ أَعۡيُنِهِمۡ لِيَقۡضِيَ ٱللَّهُ أَمۡرࣰ ا كَانَ مَفۡعُولࣰ اۗ وَإِلَى ٱللَّهِ تُرۡجَعُ ٱلۡأُمُورُ
8:44.en: And when He made you (Muslims), when ye met (them), see them with your eyes as few, and lessened you in their eyes, (it was) that Allah might conclude a thing that must be done. Unto Allah all things are brought back

15:97.ar: وَلَقَدۡ نَعۡلَمُ أَنَّكَ يَضِيقُ صَدۡرُكَ بِمَا يَقُولُونَ
15:97.en: Well know We that thy bosom is oppressed by what they say

15:98.ar: فَسَبِّحۡ بِحَمۡدِ رَبِّكَ وَكُن مِّنَ ٱلسَّٰجِدِينَ
15:98.en: But hymn the praise of thy Lord, and be of those who make prostration (unto Him)

15:99.en: And serve thy Lord till the Inevitable cometh unto thee

83:29.ar: إِنَّ ٱلَّذِينَ أَجۡرَمُواْ كَانُواْ مِنَ ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُواْ يَضۡحَكُونَ
83:29.en: Lo! the guilty used to laugh at those who believed

83:30.en: And wink one to another when they passed them

83:31.ar: وَإِذَا ٱنقَلَبُوٓاْ إِلَىٰٓ أَهۡلِهِمُ ٱنقَلَبُواْ فَكِهِينَ
83:31.en: And when they returned to their own folk, they returned jesting

83:32.ar: وَإِذَا رَأَوۡهُمۡ قَالُوٓاْ إِنَّ هَٰٓؤُلَآءِ لَضَآلُّونَ
83:32.en: And when they saw them they said: Lo! these have gone astray

83:33.en: Yet they were not sent as guardians over them

83:34.ar: فَٱلۡيَوۡمَ ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُواْ مِنَ ٱلۡكُفَّارِ يَضۡحَكُونَ
83:34.en: This day it is those who believe who have the laugh of disbelievers

83:36.ar: هَلۡ ثُوِّبَ ٱلۡكُفَّارُ مَا كَانُواْ يَفۡعَلُونَ
83:36.en: Are not the disbelievers paid for what they used to do

41:43.ar: مَّا يُقَالُ لَكَ إِلَّا مَا قَدۡ قِيلَ لِلرُّسُلِ مِن قَبۡلِكَۚ إِنَّ رَبَّكَ لَذُو مَغۡفِرَةࣲ وَذُو عِقَابٍ أَلِيمࣲ‏
41:43.en: Naught is said unto thee (Muhammad) save what was said unto the messengers before thee. Lo! thy Lord is owner of forgiveness, and owner (also) of dire punishment

qU_-0pUf63g.title: Seerah Episode 16: The Persecution of the Prophet in Makkah
qU_-0pUf63g.one_line: How Quraysh slandered, mocked and harassed the Prophet in the middle Makkan years, and how the Quran, especially Surah al-Kawthar, taught him to respond.
qU_-0pUf63g.summary: He opens the stretch of years three to eight after revelation, which is mostly persecution, and says the point is not gore but understanding what it cost for us to be born Muslim and finding our own role. He walks through the tactics Quraysh used as their arguments failed: Abu Lahab trailing the Prophet calling him insane, Nadr ibn al-Harith hired to tell Persian and Roman tales beside him, the rumour that a foreigner named Rahman was teaching him, paid youths chasing him and the insult of calling a grown man the boy of Quraysh. When ideas go bankrupt, he argues, people move to mockery and then violence. The Prophet's restraint was a conscious choice, not weakness, shown when he walked into a circle of mocking nobles and warned them. Umm Jamil's garbage and her attempt to strike him with rocks show Allah protecting him from severe humiliation by simply controlling perception. His answer to the Mudhammam poems shows him always finding something to praise. He closes with Surah al-Kawthar as a manual for being mocked: you have nothing to prove, keep praying and keep giving, and harm returns to the one who sends it. Those who wish they could have defended him should do it now by living his example.

outline.heading: Years three to eight: why tell the persecution stories
outline.gist: These years are mostly oppression of the Prophet and the companions; the aim is to see what it cost for us to be Muslim and find our own role.

outline.heading: Abu Lahab trailing the Prophet and calling him insane
outline.gist: Abu Lahab followed him to every conversation telling people he was mad, and the Prophet never even looked him in the eye.

outline.heading: Restraint as a conscious choice: repel evil with good
outline.gist: His refusal to confront was a decision not to burn bridges, taught by the verses on answering evil with what is better, not a lack of courage.

outline.heading: Quraysh losing the battle of narratives
outline.gist: His narrative and the Quran's way of arguing were stronger, and the youth were drawn to him, so Quraysh needed new tactics.

outline.heading: Nadr ibn al-Harith hired to tell rival stories
outline.gist: A well-travelled man was paid to sit beside the Prophet telling Persian and Roman legends and claim the Quran was just more fables.

outline.heading: The name ar-Rahman and why Quraysh hated it
outline.gist: Ar-Rahman was an unfamiliar, rare derivative with deep meaning that drew people to Islam, so Quraysh traced it to earlier scriptures.

outline.heading: The rumour of a foreign teacher
outline.gist: They claimed a foreigner called Rahman taught him, using the political trick of painting someone as foreign; the Quran answers with the perfection of its Arabic.

outline.heading: When arguments fail, bullies turn to mockery
outline.gist: Quraysh paid youths to run around him screaming that he was mad; he asks listeners to imagine a respected father treated this way.

outline.heading: Calling a grown man the boy of Quraysh
outline.gist: They warned visitors about the young boy of Quraysh, a term meant to belittle a grown man, which hurt him deeply.

outline.heading: Defending him today means living his example
outline.gist: Those who wish they had been there to defend him can still do so, not by shouting but by living his way, because people want examples, not information.

outline.heading: Umm Jamil dumping garbage at his door
outline.gist: Upset that Surah al-Masad named her, Abu Lahab's wife dumped her garbage at his house every morning and he cleaned it himself.

outline.heading: Umm Jamil comes with rocks and cannot see him
outline.gist: She ran to the Kaaba to strike him over the verses, explaining hija poetry, but could not see him standing beside Abu Bakr.

outline.heading: Allah controls perception: the Badr parallel
outline.gist: Allah often works through small things like perception, as at Badr where each army saw the other as fewer.

outline.heading: The Mudhammam poems
outline.gist: Umm Jamil composed catchy verses flipping his name to its opposite, and they were chanted until the companions wept.

outline.heading: They curse Mudhammam and I am Muhammad
outline.gist: He chose to see it positively; his name comes from praise, and there is always something worth praising and building on.

outline.heading: Confronting the mocking nobles after tawaf
outline.gist: After seven circuits of mockery he walked into their circle and warned them the day would come, proving he was not afraid of confrontation.

outline.heading: Your chest is tight: glorify, prostrate and keep going
outline.gist: The end of Surah al-Hijr tells him to praise, prostrate and continue until death; tasbih means not attributing flaws to Allah and focusing on improving yourself.

outline.heading: Those who sinned used to laugh at the believers
outline.gist: Surah al-Mutaffifin describes the mockers laughing at believers, a pattern still seen today, and promises the reversal on the Day of Judgment.

outline.heading: Nothing is said to you that was not said to earlier messengers
outline.gist: The Quran repeatedly tells him he is not singled out and asks him to be patient.

outline.heading: The abtar insult against Khadijah
outline.gist: Al-As ibn Wa'il mocked him for having no sons, which hurt Khadijah, and this insult alone is recorded in the Quran.

outline.heading: Al-Kawthar lesson: you have nothing to prove
outline.gist: Kawthar means the most and the best, which only Jannah can be; when people put you down you need not prove anything because Allah has already elevated you.

outline.heading: Al-Kawthar lesson: keep praying and keep giving
outline.gist: Pray and sacrifice means stay close to Allah and keep being generous to people; turning bitter after being harmed is the opposite of what the surah teaches.

outline.heading: Al-Kawthar lesson: what goes around comes around
outline.gist: The one who mocked him is forgotten and unnamed while his name endures; harm sent out gathers momentum and returns.

stories.point: He trailed the Prophet calling him insane; the Prophet never confronted or even stared him down.
Quraysh hired a storyteller to compete with the Quran, a sign they were losing the argument.
He met daily cruelty from a neighbour with patience and cleaned it up himself.
Allah preserved him from severe humiliation by simply making her unable to see him.

stories.who: The Prophet confronting the nobles at the Kaaba
stories.point: His restraint was chosen; when needed he confronted the powerful directly and alone.

stories.who: Al-As ibn Wa'il and the abtar insult
stories.point: The mocker is forgotten while the Prophet's name lives on; his own son Amr is known only through his connection to the Prophet.

takeaways: Defend the Prophet by living his example rather than by arguing loudly
Answer mistreatment with the best possible response instead of retaliating
When put down, remember you have nothing to prove before people
Keep praying and keep giving to others even after being hurt; do not turn bitter
Look for something to praise and build on in every situation
